PC: Ensure that the patient’s camera setup and positioning are optimal for physical exam, including space for them to maneuver to show the camera different aspects of the physical exam
Anticipate physical exam requirements, including positioning or uncovering certain body areas while maintaining modesty and in a manner appropriate for video platform
Ensure that patient is in a comfortable position, which may be sitting, standing or laying
Ask patient to move further away or closer to camera depending on area being examined

Begin by assessing patient’s general appearance: ill-appearing or non-toxic? Is the patient shifting position and appearing anxious or relaxed and well? Is the patient well kept in terms of personal hygiene?

Move onto assessing vital signs that can be obtained – be explicit in instructing patient how to do each of the following
Have patient check their own pulse. Have patient feel for their radial pulse and count how many beats while you time them for a given duration
While they are sitting in silence checking pulse, count their respiratory rate. Make sure that you have a good view on camera of patient’s chest rise.
If patient has ahome thermometer, ask them to check their temperature
If patient has a home blood pressure machine, ask them to check their BP
If patient has a home pulse oximeter, ask them to check their O2 saturation
If patient has a home glucometer, depending on the scenario you may choose to ask them to check a blood glucose

Move onto visually inspecting patient patient (use of each of the below may depend on scenario and history obtained – this discussion should have a different target than last)
HEENT: Check head for gross abnormalities, look to see if tongue is dry or moist, look for tongue fasciculations, attempt assessment of pupils
Neck: assess to see its supple
Lungs: Look for signs of increased respiratory effort
Heart: Assessing capillary refill in digits maybe good surrogate for overall cardiovascular status
Extremities: Look for stability of hands vs tremor, assess for how well kept the nails are or other areas of body
Skin: assess for any rash or areas of possible trauma (self-inflicted or otherwise)
Psych/Neuro: ask basic alertness and mental status questions, assess stability of gait, assess for suicidal or homicidal ideation
MK: Alcohol Withdrawal – tremors, tachycardia, recently discontinued alcohol intake with significant daily history
Depression with anxiety – Hx depression, anxious appearing, tachycardia, lack of energy,  Pulmonary Embolism - tachycardia
SBP: Appreciate the patient’s surroundings in their own home as part of your overall assessment, including perception of safety and any clues to augment the social history
Discuss your overall assessment of your patient’s safety in home environment

Make recommendations for treatment, which may include new medications, alcohol intake tapering plans, or even presenting to the closest ED.
If psych meds are considered, discuss dangers of beginning antidepressants without close follow-up
If patient is to present to the hospital, discuss whether the patient can go on their own, with social support from others close by, or there is the need to activate 911 (and how to go about doing so)
If patient is to stay at home, contract to safety and provide with emergency phone numbers for psychiatric assistance if needed.

Patient is in mild alcohol withdrawal which she has never had before. She has an unknown course through this illness and poor support structure readily available. Given difficulty to manage as outpatient, would recommend sending to emergency room for in person evaluation/treatment with benzodiazepines. It is important that a suicide evaluation is performed given initial history of depression.
ICS:
Continue to utilize and expand upon points learned from prior sessions:
Maintain proper eye contact with the camera and thus patient throughout
Obtain a detailed medical, surgical, and family history, with particular attention to the social history
SIG E CAPs utilization given concern for depression
Communicate without perceived judgement, with appropriate volume and cadence
Use hand gestures when appropriate in slow, visible fashion
Use facial expressions, smile throughout, appear engaged throughout session
Provide initial overview to the patient of the physical exam to be performed
Explain to patient the limitations of this video-based physical exam
Ensure that the patient is comfortable with what will be occurring in the physical exam
Reassure patient that they may terminate the tele-exam at any time
Summarize to the patient the findings of your history and physical exam, including the things that you feel may be important but you were not able to assess
Discuss the differential diagnosis in appropriate terms for the patient to understand
PROF:
Continue to utilize and expand upon points from prior debrief sessions:
Including proper room setup
Lighting
Background color
Camera height
Minimizing external noise

If the physical exam is limited, try to readjust and be creative in getting the needed information while maintaining a professional demeanor. Recognize that the patient is trying their best and you two are on the same team in terms of getting the needed information.
Avoid deep sighs or physical gestures that might convey frustration in this process
Verbalize any limitations in your physical exam, particularly if pertinent to final disposition planning, so that the patient is informed as to how this influences your recommendations
